1969 Dodge Super Bee Flaunts Rare A12 Package, Sold for $150K
9 photos
Photo: CARFINDER/YouTube
The 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi is arguably Chrysler's most iconic engine from the golden muscle car era. And while the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) doesn't come close in four-barrel format, the six-barrel version is a great alternative. It's also pretty rare.
Although not as scarce as a Hemi in terms of nameplate/model-year production, the 440 Six-Barrel was a short-lived powerplant. The 440 was based on the RB block, itself a raised-block variant of the B engine. The RB architecture debuted in 1959 but did not grow to 440 cubic inches until 1965.
Also known as the 440 Magnum, the performance four-barrel version came with 375 horsepower and 480 pound-feet (651 Nm) of torque on tap. Chrysler introduced the six-barrel mill for the 1969 model year. Topped by a trio of two-barrel Holley carburetors, it produced 390 horsepower and 490 pound-feet (664 Nm) of torque. The latter figure was identical to the Hemi.
The 440-6 was originally offered in only two vehicles, the Dodge Super Bee and Plymouth Road Runner . Both had been introduced as affordable muscle cars the previous year. The engine was actually part of a performance package called the A12. Dedicated to drag racers, it also included heavy-duty cooling, a Dana 60 rear end with 4.10 gears, heavy-duty brakes, and a Hemi-spec suspension setup.
In 1970, Chrysler dropped the A12 package and the six-barrel engine found its way into other B-body vehicles, including the Dodge Charger R/T and the Plymouth GTX. Availability expanded to the then-new E-body cars, the Dodge Challenger and the Plymouth Cuda. The full-size Plymouth Sport Fury GT also got it that year.
But like all high-compression Mopar V8 engines, the six-barrel was discontinued after the 1971 model year. In its short stint on the market, the powerplant found its way into fewer than 14,000 vehicles, including both Dodge and Plymouth nameplates.
The stunning Super Bee you see here is one of those cars. More importantly, it's one of those one-year-only gems that was fitted with the A12 package and not just the 440 Six-Barrel mill. It's one of 1,907 cars built for the 1969 model year and one of only 826 equipped with the four-speed manual transmission.
Finished in the spectacular high-impact Hemi Orange, the Super Bee rocks the correct fiberglass lift-off hood, and it still relies on the numbers-matching drivetrain. The same goes for the Dana rear end.
In fact, this Mopar is still highly original, despite having received a refresh a few years ago. The video below shows the Super Bee sitting pretty at Mecum's Dallas/Fort Worth 2026 auction , where it changed hands for an impressive $151,250 (including the buyer's premium). Luckily, the 440 Six-Barrel engine is also on display. Hit the play button to check it out.
